fixes.explanation: That's the one, baker. David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), says, "I will bless Your name forever and ever." He wears a crown, and he still calls God "my God and King." There's no retirement date on that praise.

I see why you'd pick that, since David was king (2 Samuel 5:3) and a reign sounds like a long time. But David doesn't put a term limit on it. He says, "I will bless Your name forever and ever." That runs way past any crown he'll ever wear.

David fought battles as king (2 Samuel 8:1), so that's a fair thing to think of. But he never says his praise ends when the fighting does. He says, "I will bless Your name forever and ever." Battles come to an end, but this praise doesn't have a finish line, friend.

Feasts and victories are natural times to cheer, so I get the guess. But David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), says, "Every day I will bless You, and I will praise Your name forever and ever." That means the plain Tuesdays count too. Even the Tuesday when nothing happens and the oven is making a weird noise.

Yes, baker. David says, "One generation will commend Your works to the next, and will proclaim Your mighty acts…" He's picturing the news getting passed down, one group to the next. It's like a recipe handed down from one cook to the next, except this news is the best thing to pass along.

Tribe is a reasonable guess for a king who ruled over Israel (2 Samuel 5:3). But David says, "One generation will commend Your works to the next…" He's looking at who comes after, not at who sits beside him. That's why the word is generation.

That one makes sense, since the psalm is full of praise. But David doesn't put a condition on it. He says, "The LORD is good to all; His compassion rests on all He has made." The words he picks are all and all He has made.

David was a king on earth (2 Samuel 5:3), so it's easy to think that way. But he says, "Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and Your dominion endures through all generations." He doesn't call it earthly. He says it lasts.

Growing is a nice word for a kingdom. But that isn't the word David uses. He says, "Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and Your dominion endures through all generations." What he says about it is that it's everlasting and endures.

Right on, baker. David says, "The LORD is faithful in all His words and kind in all His actions." All His words, not most of them. Most of us keep our word right up until the snooze button gets involved.

The Sabbath mattered to God's people (Exodus 20:8), so that's a fair guess. But in this verse David says, "The LORD is near to all who call on Him, to all who call out to Him in truth." What he names is calling on the LORD in truth.

Serving in the temple sounds close to God, so I see why you picked it. But David doesn't say that here. He says, "The LORD is near to all who call on Him, to all who call out to Him in truth." He names those who call out in truth.

That's right, baker. David says, "He fulfills the desires of those who fear Him; He hears their cry and saves them." The LORD hears and the LORD saves. I know a little about crying out from the back of a dark junk drawer where I sat for years, and this verse hits home.

Priests are the ones we picture leading worship, so that's a sensible guess. But David ends with, "let every creature bless His holy name forever and ever." He isn't leaving the praise to a few people with the job. He calls on every creature.
